newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy passes data protection law, step to Schengen.
newsitem.headline: Italy passes data protection law, step to Schengen.

text.p: Italy has passed a law guaranteeing the protection of personal data 15 years after debate began in parliament, clearing a key hurdle in its bid to become a full member of the Schengen group of open border countries in Europe.

The law, governing limits on the type of information the state can hold on citizens and restrictions on its use, was passed with cross-party support by the Chamber of Deputies justice commission on Wednesday.

Approval by the commission, giving the measures force of law, was warmly welcomed by the centre-left government, which hopes Italy will be able to join the Schengen group of seven countries within the European Union by next March.
Measures in the law include provisions for a privacy watchdog authority, to which Italians can turn for access to data stored on them.
Passage of the data protection law was one of the requirements for full membership of Schengen, which provides for a system of open borders and passport-free movement.
Another is the construction of special walkways for Schengen group nationals at ports, airports and border points.
"Italy now has all its cards in order for joining the operational Schengen group," deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino said.

Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano and Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick issued a joint statement welcoming passage of the bill "positively concluding a debate and legislative passage that has been under way now for 15 years".
"It puts Italy in line with European standards in terms of the protection of private lives, particularly in relation to the development of information technology," they said.

France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain, Portugal and Germany are all full Schengen members. Greece and Austria, like Italy, have also signed the accord but have yet to put the required legislation in place.
